title: Animal babies: how they grow up, and how they are cared for

summary.text: A sparrow chick in a dark hole in the wall cannot see the parent coming. Yet the parent finds the chick's mouth every time. Young animals grow and change until they are adults, and many need care on the way: food, warmth and safety. Some babies can walk within an hour of birth, and some need years of care, like human babies. Your child makes a dark nest of paper chick mouths and tests which mouth colours a parent finds and feeds first.
summary.art: A hole in a city wall with two open chick mouths inside, each with bright yellow edges, and a brown sparrow arriving with an insect in her beak.

intro.hook: Sparrow chicks live in a dark hole in a wall. When a parent flies in with food, how does the parent find the right place to put it?
intro.text: Every animal starts small and grows into an adult. A calf can stand on the day she is born. A sparrow chick hatches with no feathers and shut eyes. A human baby cannot even sit up for months. Babies like these need someone to look after them. But babies are not only waiting to be cared for. They call, beg, cry and open their mouths wide. In this unit you find out how babies help their own care. You test it with a dark nest full of paper mouths.
intro.art: Side by side: a calf standing next to a cow in a field, a bare sparrow chick with shut eyes in a nest, and a human baby lying on a mat.

outcomes: By the end I can say how young animals, including humans, change as they grow into adults.
By the end I can say which babies can walk soon after birth, and which need a lot of care.
By the end I can name ways that parents and other helpers care for young: feeding, keeping warm, keeping safe, cleaning and teaching.
By the end I can say how babies help their own care: by begging, calling, crying, holding on and showing bright mouths.
By the end I can make a guess with a reason, test a dark nest fairly, count the results and say what I found.
By the end I can say that humans are animals, and that human young need care for longer than most animals.

terms.meaning: An adult is an animal who has finished growing up.
terms.example: A hen is an adult. Her chicks are her young. Your parents and grandparents are adults.
terms.art: A hen standing with three small yellow chicks around her feet.

terms.meaning: Growth is the way a young animal gets bigger and changes as they get older.
terms.example: A kitten's growth: she gets bigger, opens her eyes, grows teeth and learns to hunt.
terms.art: A row of four drawings: a newborn kitten with shut eyes, a kitten with open eyes, a playing kitten and a grown cat.

terms.meaning: Care is what parents and helpers do to keep young animals alive and well: feeding, keeping warm, keeping safe, cleaning and teaching.
terms.example: A mother cow licks her new calf clean and feeds her milk. That is care.
terms.art: A cow licking a newborn calf in a shed, the calf standing on wobbly legs.

terms.meaning: Begging is how young animals ask for food. They call, open their mouths wide, flap their wings or cry.
terms.example: Sparrow chicks beg by stretching up, cheeping and opening their mouths wide when a parent arrives.
terms.art: Three sparrow chicks in a nest stretching up with wide open mouths and a parent above them.

terms.meaning: The gape is a chick's open mouth. Many chicks have a bright colour inside the mouth, or bright edges around it.
terms.example: A sparrow chick's gape has bright yellow edges. A crow chick's mouth is red inside.
terms.art: Close-up of a chick's open mouth from the front, with bright yellow edges at the corners.

terms.meaning: Brooding is when a parent bird sits over eggs or small chicks to keep them warm.
terms.example: A hen brooding her chicks spreads her wings, and the chicks tuck in underneath.
terms.art: A hen sitting with wings spread a little, and chick heads peeping out from under her feathers.

terms.meaning: A mammal is an animal with hair or fur whose mother feeds the young on milk.
terms.example: Cows, cats, bats, elephants and humans are mammals. A newborn mammal drinks milk first.
terms.art: A goat feeding her kid milk, and beside them a mother holding a baby.

explanations.concept: Growing up means getting bigger and changing
explanations.context: This card is about what changes when a young animal grows into an adult.
explanations.definition: Growth is how a young animal gets bigger and changes until they become an adult.
explanations.description: Young animals get bigger as they grow, and they also change. A kitten is born with her eyes shut. They open after about one to two weeks, and later she grows teeth and learns to hunt. A human baby has no teeth and cannot walk or talk. Then teeth grow, the baby walks at about one year old and starts to talk.
examples: A puppy opens their eyes after about two weeks.
A chick's fluff is replaced by feathers.
A human baby grows teeth, then walks, then talks.
A tadpole grows legs and becomes a frog.
explanations.art: A row of human stages: a baby lying down, a toddler walking, a child of 7, a teenager, an adult and a grandmother.

explanations.concept: Born ready, or born needing care
explanations.context: This card is about how much a baby animal can do on the first day of life.
explanations.definition: Some young animals can walk and feed soon after birth. Others are born helpless and need a lot of care.
explanations.description: A calf stands up within about an hour of birth and soon follows her mother. A goat kid, a duckling and a hen's chick can walk within a day. A sparrow chick hatches with almost no feathers and shut eyes. A newborn kitten cannot see or walk properly. A human baby cannot even hold up their head at first, and needs years of care. Humans have one of the longest childhoods of any animal.
examples: Born ready: a calf, a goat kid, a hen's chick, a duckling, a baby gecko.
Born needing care: a kitten, a puppy, a sparrow chick, a crow chick, a baby mouse, a human baby.
explanations.art: Two groups: on the left a calf standing and a chick pecking, on the right a bare sparrow chick in a nest and a human baby in a cradle.

explanations.concept: How young animals are cared for
explanations.context: This card is about the ways that parents, and other helpers, look after young animals.
explanations.definition: Care means feeding the young, keeping them warm, keeping them safe, keeping them clean and teaching them.
explanations.description: Parents feed their young. Mammal mothers make milk, and sparrow parents bring insects to the nest many times an hour. A hen keeps her chicks warm under her wings, and a crow will dive at a person who comes near the nest. Often more than one carer helps. Both sparrow parents feed the chicks, and langur aunts take turns holding a baby. In a honeybee hive, older sisters feed the young. Human babies are cared for by parents, grandparents, aunts, older brothers and sisters, and friends.
examples: A hen keeps her chicks warm under her wings.
Langur aunts take turns holding a baby.
Worker bees feed the young bees in the hive.
A grandmother feeds a baby ragi porridge.
explanations.art: A langur mother sitting on a temple wall while another female langur holds her baby, and a third langur reaches out to the baby.

explanations.context: This card is about the things babies do to get looked after.
explanations.definition: Young animals send signals that tell carers what they need: begging calls, open mouths, crying, holding on and smiling.
explanations.description: A sparrow chick stretches up, cheeps and opens a wide yellow-edged mouth when a parent lands. A hungry chick begs harder than a full one. A puppy whimpers when cold or alone, and a baby langur holds on tight to the fur of whoever carries them. A human baby cries when hungry and grips a finger that touches their palm. By about six weeks old, most human babies smile at the faces around them. Each signal helps a carer know what to do next, so care is something the baby and the carer do together.
examples: A chick opens a bright mouth wide.
A kitten mews when she is away from her mother.
A human baby cries, grips and smiles.
A baby langur clings to fur.
explanations.art: A grandmother holding a smiling baby who is gripping her finger tightly.

explanations.concept: Why are chick mouths so bright?
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: why so many chicks have brightly coloured mouths.
explanations.description: Many chicks have bright mouths. Sparrow chicks have yellow edges around the mouth. Crow chicks are red inside the mouth. Scientists have tested two main ideas, and the answer may be different for different birds.
examples: House sparrow chicks: bright yellow mouth edges, in nests inside holes.
Crow chicks: a red mouth inside, in open nests of sticks.
In your dark nest test, yellow paper mouths were found more often than dark ones.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study nests in holes
perspectives.explanation: Bright mouths are easy to find in a dark nest. In a test in 2003, scientists painted the mouths of great tit chicks yellow or red. In dim nests, the parents fed the yellow-painted chicks more. In bright nests, colour made no difference.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study barn swallows and other birds
perspectives.explanation: The colour of the mouth tells the parent something about the chick, such as how hungry or how healthy they are. In some of these birds, parents feed chicks with redder mouths more.

explanations.art: Two nests side by side: a dark hole in a wall with chicks showing yellow-edged mouths, and an open stick nest in a tree with crow chicks showing red mouths.

agreed.text: Every kind of animal has young, and the young grow and change until they are adults. Humans are one kind of animal, and grow the same way.
agreed.evidence: People have watched the young of thousands of kinds of animals grow up, from ants to elephants. A kitten always becomes a cat, and a human baby always becomes an adult human.

agreed.text: Some young animals can walk and feed within hours of birth, and others are born helpless and need care for a long time.
agreed.evidence: Farmers see calves and goat kids stand within an hour of birth. Sparrow and crow chicks hatch with shut eyes and almost no feathers, and stay in the nest for about two weeks or more.

agreed.text: Young animals beg, call or cry, and parents answer these signals with food and care.
agreed.evidence: Scientists who watch nests see that chicks beg when a parent arrives. When chicks are hungrier, they beg harder, and parents usually bring food more often.

challenging.for: In most mammals, like cats and cows, the mother does almost all the care. Only mother mammals make milk.
challenging.against: Sparrow fathers feed the chicks about as often as the mothers do. Langur aunts hold babies. Worker bees, who are sisters, feed young bees. Human babies are cared for by many people: fathers, grandparents, aunts and older children.
challenging.context: This card is about who does the caring.

challenging.claim: If a person touches a baby bird, the parents will smell the person and leave the chick.
challenging.who: A very common belief, told to many children
challenging.for: It is true that people should not touch nests or chicks. Disturbing a nest can scare the parents, and the chicks can get hurt.
challenging.against: Most small birds have a weak sense of smell. Scientists who must handle chicks, to weigh them, find that the parents come back and keep feeding them. Still, leave nests alone and watch from far away.
challenging.context: This card is about a belief that is wrong, though the advice behind it is good.

challenging.claim: A parent and a baby always want the same thing.
challenging.for: Parents and babies both need the baby to grow up safe and well.
challenging.against: In 1974 an American scientist, Robert Trivers, pointed out that a chick may beg for more food than the parent wants to give. The parent also needs food, and may have other young. Scientists still argue about how much parents and young pull against each other.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument among scientists.

challenging.who: Many baby doctors and scientists, about 70 years ago
challenging.for: Babies do feel calm and happy after a feed, with the person who fed them.
challenging.against: Mary Ainsworth in Uganda, and Rudolph Schaffer and Peggy Emerson in Scotland, watched babies closely. Babies held on most to the people who answered them: who came when they cried, talked and played with them. That was often, but not always, the person who fed them.
challenging.context: This card is about a wrong idea about babies, and how it was tested.

big_questions.q: When a baby cries and a grown-up picks them up, who started the caring: the baby or the grown-up?
big_questions.hint: Think about the dark nest test. Did the paper mouths do anything to get fed? What do real chicks do?

big_questions.q: Why does a human child need so many years of care, when a calf can walk on the first day?
big_questions.hint: Think about all the things you have learnt since you were a baby. Could a calf learn all of them?

big_questions.q: What might a sparrow parent feel when the chicks beg?
big_questions.hint: Think about how you feel when a small child asks you for help.

big_questions.q: You were cared for by many people. Who are you caring for now?
big_questions.hint: A plant, a pet, a younger cousin, a friend, a grandparent: caring can go both ways.

big_questions.q: You grew from a baby into a child of seven. Are you the same person as that baby?
big_questions.hint: What has changed about you? Is anything still the same?

story.title: The Yellow Mouths in the Meter Box
story.note: A made-up story. House sparrows really do nest in holes in walls and behind meter boxes. Both parents feed the chicks, the chicks have bright yellow mouth edges, and they leave the nest at about two weeks old.
text: Kavya lived on the second floor of a building in Kochi. She was seven. Her cousin Rahul, who was six, came to stay for the summer holidays.

On the stairs outside their flat there was a grey electricity box, with a gap above it in the wall. One morning Kavya saw a small brown bird fly into the gap. The bird had a long piece of dry grass in her beak.
'That is a female sparrow,' said Ammachi, Kavya's grandmother. 'She is plain brown. The male has a black patch under his beak. They are making a nest in the wall.'
Ammachi gave Kavya an old notebook. 'If you want to watch them, sit on the top step. That is far enough. If you come close, they will be scared to go in.'

So every morning, Kavya and Rahul sat on the top step with the notebook. The two sparrows carried in grass, feathers and a bit of thread. Then, for many days, they were very quiet. One of them was usually inside.
'They are sitting on eggs,' said Ammachi. 'They keep the eggs warm, so that the chicks can grow inside.'

About two weeks later, Kavya heard a sound from the wall. It was a tiny, thin cheep, cheep, cheep. Now the parents never stopped. The mother flew in with a green caterpillar. The father flew in with a moth. Out they came, and off they went again.
'How many times do they come?' asked Rahul.

Kavya looked at the clock in the hall. For ten minutes, she made a mark in the notebook every time a parent went in. When the ten minutes were up, she counted. 'Eight times!' she said. 'Four for the mother and four for the father.'
'That is a lot of caterpillars,' said Rahul.
'Chicks grow very fast,' said Ammachi. 'They need a lot of food. When they hatch, they have no feathers, and their eyes are shut. They cannot even hold up their heads for long.'
Kavya frowned. 'It is so dark in that hole. The parents come in from the bright sunlight. How do they know where to put the food?'
Ammachi smiled. 'Watch carefully. Maybe the chicks will show you.'

A few days later, Ammachi held up her phone. She zoomed the camera into the gap, from the top step. On the screen, in the dark, Kavya saw three round shapes. Each had two bright yellow corners, like little yellow lamps. Then the mother landed, and all three shapes opened wide. They were mouths! The yellow edges shone around each open mouth. The mother pushed her caterpillar into the widest one.
'The yellow is the edge of their mouths,' said Kavya. 'In the dark, the yellow is the easiest thing to see.'
'So the chicks are helping,' said Rahul. 'They are showing the mother where to put the food.'
'Yes,' said Ammachi. 'And they cheep louder when they are hungry. The parents listen.'
Kavya wrote in the notebook: 'The chicks are not just waiting. They beg. They open yellow mouths. The parents follow the yellow.'

Each day the chicks grew. Soon their cheeps were loud enough to hear from inside the flat. One morning, Kavya saw a small head poking out of the gap. The chick had short brown feathers now. The yellow corners of the mouth were still there.

Then, one day, there was a chick sitting on the stair railing, fluffing out their feathers. The chick could fly a little, but not far. The father sparrow landed next to them. The chick shivered their wings and opened their yellow mouth wide. The father fed them a moth.
'The chick has left the nest, and the father is still feeding them,' said Kavya.
'Young birds keep begging for a while after they leave the nest,' said Ammachi. 'The parents keep feeding them until the young ones learn to find food by themselves.'
That evening, Rahul's mother rang from Bengaluru. Rahul told her all about the sparrows. 'Kavya says I was a baby who begged too,' he said. 'I cried, and you came.'
His mother laughed. 'You did. You cried very loudly. And you held my finger so tight, I could not let go.'
Kavya drew one last picture in the notebook. It showed a dark hole, three yellow mouths, and a sparrow flying in. Under it she wrote: 'Who did the caring? Everyone did.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: Kavya notices that the chicks are not only cared for. They beg, cheep and show bright mouths, and the parents answer. She also sees that both parents feed the chicks, and that the care goes on after the chicks leave the nest.
ask: Why were the yellow edges of the chicks' mouths easy to see?
How did Kavya find out how often the parents brought food?
How did Rahul help his own mother look after him when he was a baby?
art: A girl and a younger boy sitting on the top step of a stairway in a Kochi building, looking at a grey electricity box with a gap above it, while a sparrow flies in with grass.
A girl making tally marks in a notebook while a sparrow flies into a gap in the wall.
A phone screen showing a dark hole with three open chick mouths, each with bright yellow corners.
A brown fluffy sparrow chick on a stair railing with a wide yellow-edged mouth, and the father sparrow, with a black patch under his beak, feeding the chick a moth.

experiments.title: Find the Hungry Mouth: which chick gets fed in a dark nest?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a nest of paper chick mouths in four colours. In a dim room, you play the parent bird and feed every mouth you can find. Then you count which colours got fed most.
experiments.question: In a dark nest, which colour of chick mouth does a parent find and feed most often?
experiments.predict: Guess first. In the dim nest, which colour of mouth will you feed most: yellow, orange, brown or black? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All the mouths are the same size, and there are two of each colour. The grown-up mixes them up before every round, so no colour is always in the best place. Each round lasts the same 10 seconds. We do three rounds in dim light, because one round can be luck. Then one round in bright light, to see if the light makes a difference.

materials.item: a dark cloth, such as a black or brown dupatta, an old dark towel or a dark bedsheet
a shoebox, a steel plate with a rim, or a large kadai, to be the nest
paper, and crayons or sketch pens in yellow, orange, brown and black
a bottle cap or a one-rupee coin, to draw round circles
dried chana, rajma or small paper balls, to be the food
children's scissors, and a pencil and paper for the results

experiments.safety: Keep the chana away from toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Make 8 paper mouths, line the nest, then feed the mouths in dim light three times and in bright light once. Count and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table with the number of chana on each colour. Draw a block for each chana under each colour to make a block graph.

setup.art: Eight paper circles the size of a bottle cap on a table: two yellow, two orange, two brown and two black, with crayons and scissors beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Make 8 paper mouths: 2 yellow, 2 orange, 2 brown, 2 black.

setup.art: A shoebox lined with a dark brown cloth, with the eight paper circles scattered on the cloth.
setup.caption: 2. Line the nest with dark cloth and scatter the mouths.

setup.art: A dim room with curtains closed and a child bending over the box, putting a chana onto a yellow circle, while a grown-up counts on her fingers.
setup.caption: 3. In dim light, put one chana on each mouth you can find, in 10 seconds.

setup.art: The box in bright light with chana on the paper circles, most on the yellow ones, and a child counting.
setup.caption: 4. Switch on the light and count the chana on each colour.

flow.do: 1. Draw round a bottle cap 8 times on paper. 2. Colour 2 circles yellow, 2 orange, 2 brown and 2 black. Colour them fully. 3. Cut them out.
flow.say: These circles are chick mouths. Real chicks have mouths of different colours. Let's make yellow, orange, brown and black ones.
flow.kid: Draw 8 circles. Colour 2 yellow, 2 orange, 2 brown, 2 black. Cut them out.
flow.parent: Colour the black and brown circles fully, so no white paper shows. A sketch pen works well.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess which colour they will feed most in the dark, and why. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Soon the room will be dim, like a nest in a hole. You are the parent bird. Which mouths will you feed most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which colour will you feed most in the dark? Why?

good: Yellow, because yellow is bright.
Black, because it looks like a dark mouth.
All the same, because I will look carefully.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine, as long as there is a reason. Do not tell your child what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Line the box or kadai with the dark cloth. 2. Your child looks away. 3. Scatter the 8 mouths on the cloth, apart from each other. 4. Close the curtains and switch off the lights.
flow.say: Close your eyes while I make the nest. Now the room is dim, like a hole in a wall. Can you still see a little?
flow.kid: Look away while the nest is made. Now the room goes dim.
flow.parent: The room should be dim, not pitch dark. Your child should just about see the box. Evening with the curtains shut and a light on in another room works well. In daytime, put the box under a table and cover the table with a bedsheet.

flow.do: 1. Give your child 10 chana. 2. Say 'Go!' and count to 10 out loud. 3. Your child puts one chana on each mouth they find. 4. Switch on the light, count the chana on each colour, write the numbers in the table, and pick up all the chana. 5. Mix the mouths while your child looks away, and make the room dim again. 6. Repeat. Do 3 rounds in all.
flow.say: Ready, parent bird? You have ten seconds to feed every mouth you can find. One chana on each mouth. Go!
flow.kid: Put one chana on each mouth you see. Be quick! Then count.

ask.q: Which mouths were easy to find?
good: The yellow ones. They stood out.
The black ones were hard. They looked like the cloth.

flow.parent: A chana put on the cloth does not count. Mix the mouths well each time, with your child looking away. Usually yellow mouths get the most chana, then orange. Black and brown are often missed, because they are hard to see against the dark cloth. Each mouth can get only one chana, so a colour can get at most 2 in a round and 6 in three rounds. If every colour is found in every round, the room is too bright: make it dimmer. If your result is different, that is a real result too: talk about why.

flow.do: 1. Switch the lights on and open the curtains. 2. Mix the mouths. 3. Do one more round of 10 seconds in bright light. 4. Count the chana on each colour.
flow.say: Now let's do it once in bright light. Will the colour still matter?
flow.kid: Now try in bright light. Is every mouth easy to find?
flow.parent: In bright light, your child will usually find almost every mouth, whatever the colour. This shows that the colour matters most when the nest is dark.

flow.do: 1. Add up the dim-light rounds for each colour. 2. Your child draws one block for each chana, to make a block graph. 3. Ask what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Which colour got fed most in the dark? Was your guess right? Why do you think that colour did best?
flow.kid: Add up. Which colour got the most food? Why?

ask.q: Why did that colour get the most food?
good: Yellow is easy to see in the dark.
The black mouths looked like the cloth, so I missed them.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the numbers: 'Yellow got 5 chana and black got 1, because yellow shows up in the dark.' Now read the card on why chick mouths are so bright.

check.q: Sparrow chicks live in dark holes in walls. Why are yellow mouth edges useful to them?
options: Yellow edges keep the chicks warm
A parent can find yellow edges easily in the dark
Yellow edges make the food taste better
check.why: In your dim nest, yellow mouths were found and fed more than dark ones. A parent coming into a dark hole can find bright yellow edges quickly. If you picked warmth, remember that the colour only changed how easy the mouths were to see.

activities.title: The Walking Line: how soon can each baby walk?
activities.context: In this activity you lay a long line of string across the floor, from 'just born' to 'two years old'. You guess where each baby animal goes on the line: when can they first walk? Then you check.

materials.item: a long string, a dupatta or a line of newspaper sheets across the floor
6 small cards with a baby drawn on each: calf, hen's chick, kitten, puppy, human baby, goat kid

schedule.what: Lay the walking line, guess where each baby goes, then check and talk.

activities.record: Draw the line in your notebook with each baby in the right place.

setup.art: A string across a floor, with a paper label 'just born' at one end and 'two years' at the other end, and small marks for 'one hour', 'one day', 'one month' and 'one year'.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a line from 'just born' to 'two years old'.

setup.art: A child placing small cards of a calf, a goat kid, a chick, a kitten, a puppy and a human baby along the string.
setup.caption: 2. Put each baby where you think they first walk.

flow.do: 1. Lay the string across the room. 2. Put a paper at one end saying 'just born'. 3. Put papers along it: 'one hour', 'one day', 'one month', 'one year', and 'two years' at the far end.
flow.say: This line is time. Here is the day a baby is born. Over there, the baby is two years old.
flow.kid: This line is time. One end is birth. The far end is two years.

flow.do: Your child puts each baby card where they think that baby first walks.
flow.say: When does each baby first walk? Put each card on the line. Why did you put the calf there?
flow.kid: Put each baby where they first walk. Say why.

ask.q: Why did you put that baby there?
good: The calf goes near the start, because calves walk quickly.
The human baby goes far along, because babies take a long time.

flow.do: Read out the real answers and move the cards: calf and goat kid, about one hour. Chick, the first day. Kitten and puppy, about three weeks. Human baby, about one year.
flow.say: A calf stands within about an hour, and so does a goat kid. A chick walks on the first day. A kitten and a puppy walk at about three weeks. A human baby walks at about one year.
flow.kid: Move the cards to the right places. Who walks first? Who walks last?
flow.parent: Human babies walk at different ages, often between about 9 and 18 months. All of these are normal. The point is the big difference between the calf and the human baby.

flow.do: Talk about why some babies walk so early.
flow.say: A calf must follow her mother, who walks to find grass. Why can a human baby take so long?
flow.kid: Why can a human baby take so long to walk?

ask.q: Why can a human baby take so long?
good: Because people carry the baby.
Because the family looks after the baby.

check.why: A calf stands within about an hour of birth. A kitten walks at about three weeks, and a human baby at about one year.

activities.title: My First Food: ask the family
activities.context: In this activity you ask the grown-ups at home what you ate and drank when you were a baby, and who fed you. You find out how a baby's food changes as the baby grows.

materials.item: a grown-up at home, or on the phone, who remembers you as a baby

schedule.what: Ask a grown-up four questions, write or draw the answers, and put your foods in order.

activities.record: A page with three pictures: my first food, my food when I was one, my food now.

setup.art: A girl with a notebook asking a grown-up questions, the grown-up smiling and holding up a small steel bowl.
setup.caption: 1. Ask a grown-up what you ate as a baby.

setup.art: A notebook page with three drawings in a row: a baby drinking milk, a small bowl of ragi porridge, and a plate of idli and sambar.
setup.caption: 2. Draw your foods in order.

flow.do: Your child asks a grown-up these questions: 1. What did I drink first? 2. What was my first solid food? 3. When did I start eating what the family eats? 4. Who fed me?
flow.say: You are a scientist asking questions. Ask your question, then listen to the whole answer before the next one.
flow.kid: Ask your grown-up four questions. Listen to each answer.
flow.parent: Many Indian families start babies on milk only, then soft foods at about six months, such as ragi porridge, mashed rice with dal, or mashed banana. Any true answer is good.

flow.do: Your child draws or writes the answers in order: first food, food at about one year, food now.
flow.say: Draw your first food, then your food when you were one, then your food now. What changed?
flow.kid: Draw your three foods in order. What changed?

ask.q: Why does a baby eat soft food?
good: Because I had no teeth.
Because a baby cannot chew hard food.

flow.do: Ask your child who fed them as a baby, and who or what they feed or help now.
flow.say: Many people fed you. Is there anyone, or any plant or pet, that you feed now?
flow.kid: Who fed you? Who do you feed or help now?

activities.title: Nest Watch from the Window (if you can see a nest)
activities.context: If you can see a bird's nest from your window or balcony, watch it for 10 minutes and count how often the parents bring food. Sparrows, mynas, pigeons and crows often nest near flats, mostly from February to June.

materials.item: a window or balcony from which you can see a nest
a notebook, a pencil and a clock or phone

activities.safety: Watch from far away and never touch a nest. Crows dive at people who come close to their nest.

schedule.what: Watch a nest for 10 minutes. Make a tally mark each time a parent arrives. Count.

activities.record: A tally of parent visits in 10 minutes, and a drawing of the nest.

setup.art: A child at a window with a notebook, looking at a crow's nest of sticks in a tree outside.
setup.caption: 1. Find a nest you can see from far away.

setup.art: A notebook page with tally marks in groups of five and a small clock drawn beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Make a mark each time a parent arrives.

flow.do: Find a nest you can see from inside. Sit still and quiet.
flow.say: We will watch from here, so the parents are not scared. Can you see the nest?
flow.kid: Sit still. Find the nest. Don't go close.

flow.do: Watch for 10 minutes. Your child makes one tally mark each time a parent arrives with food.
flow.say: Each time a parent lands at the nest, make a mark. Can you hear the chicks when the parent comes?
flow.kid: Make a mark each time a parent comes. Listen for the chicks.
flow.parent: If no parent comes in 10 minutes, that is a result too. Try again at another time of day. Early morning is often busy.

flow.do: Count the marks and talk about it.
flow.say: How many times did a parent come? What did the chicks do when a parent arrived?
flow.kid: Count your marks. What did the chicks do?

ask.q: What did the chicks do when a parent arrived?
good: They called louder.
They stretched up and opened their mouths.

activities.title: Who Grows Up Fastest? Baby to grown-up cards
activities.context: In this activity you put animals in order by how long they take to grow up, from a mouse to a human. You compare their growing-up time with your own age.

materials.item: 5 small cards with these written and drawn: a mouse, a dog, a cow, an elephant, a human

schedule.what: Order the animal cards by growing-up time, check, and compare with your own age.

activities.record: Write the five animals in order in your notebook.

setup.art: Five cards on a floor: a mouse, a dog, a cow, an elephant and a human, with a child's hand moving one card.
setup.caption: 1. Put the animals in order: who grows up fastest?

setup.art: The same five cards in a row from mouse to human, with short labels: about 2 months, 1 to 2 years, about 2 years, about 15 years, about 18 years.
setup.caption: 2. Check the real times.

flow.do: Your child puts the cards in order, from the animal who grows up fastest to the slowest.
flow.say: Which of these animals grows up fastest? Which takes the longest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put them in order. Who grows up fastest? Who takes longest?

flow.do: Read the answers. A mouse is grown up in about two months. A dog in about one to two years. A cow in about two years. An elephant in about 15 years. A human in about 18 years.
flow.say: A mouse is grown up in about two months. A dog in about one or two years. A cow in about two years. An elephant takes about 15 years. A human takes about 18 years.
flow.kid: Check your order. Were you right?
flow.parent: A dog and a cow are close: either order is fine for those two.

flow.do: Compare with your child's age. Ask how old they are, and how many years are left until 18.
flow.say: How old are you? A dog of that age is already a grown-up. How many more years until you are 18?
flow.kid: How old are you? How many years until you are 18?

check.q: Which animal takes longest to grow up?
check.why: Humans take about 18 years to grow up. A dog takes one or two years, and a mouse only about two months.

games.title: Ready or Needs Help?
games.context: This is a sorting race about baby animals. Some babies can walk and feed soon after birth. Others need a lot of care. Players turn over baby cards and race to the right mat.

printables.title: 16 baby animal cards to cut out, with the answer on the back

items.b: Ready. A calf stands within about an hour and follows her mother.
Ready. A goat kid stands and drinks milk within about an hour.
Ready. A chick walks and pecks on the day she hatches. Her mother still keeps her warm.
Ready. A duckling walks and swims within a day of hatching.
Ready. A baby gecko hatches and hunts insects alone.
Ready. Most baby fish swim off and feed alone.
Ready. An elephant calf stands within a few hours, but drinks milk and learns from the herd for years.

img.credit: Morten Ross, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Ready. Baby spiders hatch and soon spread out to live alone.
Needs help. A newborn kitten has shut eyes and cannot walk properly.
Needs help. A newborn puppy has shut eyes and drinks only milk.
Needs help. A sparrow chick hatches with almost no feathers and shut eyes.
Needs help. A crow chick is fed by both parents in the nest for weeks.
Needs help. A baby mouse is born pink, with no fur and shut eyes.
Needs help. A bat pup clings to the mother and drinks her milk.
Needs help. A young bee is a tiny grub, fed by older sister bees.
Needs help. A human baby cannot hold up their head at first, and needs care for years.

printables.title: 2 mats to lay on the floor

rules: Draw a quick baby on the front of each card, next to the name.
Lay the two mats on the floor, a little apart.
Mix the cards and put them face down in a pile.
One player turns over the top card and reads the name aloud.
Everyone, including the reader, races to put a hand on the right mat. A hand on the wrong mat means you sit out that card.
Turn the card over and read the back aloud to check. The first hand on the right mat wins the card. If nobody was right, put the card at the bottom of the pile.
Take turns to be the reader. When the pile is finished, the player with the most cards wins. If two players have the same number, they both win.

flow.do: 1. Share the 16 cards and draw a quick baby on each. 2. Lay the two mats on the floor.
flow.say: Let's draw the babies first. You draw some, and I will draw some.
flow.kid: Draw a baby on your cards. Then lay out the two mats.

flow.do: 1. Take turns turning over a card. 2. Race to the right mat. 3. Read the back aloud.
flow.say: Kitten! Ready, or needs help? Quick!
flow.kid: Turn over a card. Slap the right mat. Read the back.

ask.q: The hen's chick can walk, but her mother still keeps her warm. Which mat is she on?
good: Ready, because she can walk and peck.
Ready, but she still needs some care.

flow.parent: The tricky cards are the chick and the elephant calf. They can walk early, but still get care. Let your child argue for their choice.

flow.do: Count the cards.
flow.say: Which mat is the human baby on? Count your cards.
flow.kid: Count your cards. Which mat is the human baby on?

check.q: Which baby needs the most help after birth?
check.why: A sparrow chick hatches with almost no feathers and shut eyes, and must be fed in the nest. A calf and a duckling can walk within a day.

setup.art: Sixteen small cards with baby animals drawn on them, in a pile on a floor.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a baby on each card.

setup.art: Two paper mats on a floor, one saying 'Ready soon after birth' and one saying 'Needs a lot of help', with two children's hands racing towards them.
setup.caption: 2. Turn a card and race to the right mat.

games.title: Who Looks After Me? A memory game
games.context: This is a memory game with pairs of cards. Each baby card has a matching card that shows who looks after that baby. Find the pairs, and learn who the carers are.

printables.title: 16 cards to cut out: 8 babies and 8 carers
items: Carer: the mother hen, who keeps the chicks warm under her wings
Carer: both sparrow parents, who bring insects many times an hour
Carer: the mother, and the other female langurs, who take turns holding the baby
Carer: the worker bees, the baby's older sisters, who feed the young
Carer: the mother cow, who licks the calf clean and feeds her milk
Carer: the mother king cobra, who builds a nest of leaves and guards the eggs
Carer: the mother tilapia, who keeps her babies safe inside her mouth
Carer: many people: parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles and older children

rules: Mix all 16 cards and lay them face down in rows of four.
On your turn, turn over two cards and read them aloud.
If you turn over a baby and the carer of that baby, you keep the pair and have another turn.
If they do not match, turn them face down again. The next player has a turn.
When all the pairs are found, the player with the most pairs wins. If two players have the same number, they both win.

flow.do: Mix the cards and lay them face down in four rows of four.
flow.say: Each baby has a card that says who looks after them. Let's find the pairs.
flow.kid: Lay the cards face down in rows.

flow.do: Take turns turning over two cards. Read them aloud. Keep a matching pair.
flow.say: A tilapia fish and a hen. Is that a pair? Why not?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Do they match?

good: The tilapia mother keeps babies in her mouth!
The bees are fed by their sisters.

flow.parent: Talk about each pair as it is found. The king cobra is one of the few snakes that builds a nest. Many people help raise a human baby.

flow.do: Count the pairs. Talk about who cared for your child.
flow.say: Who looked after you when you were a baby? Is that more like the hen, or more like the langurs?
flow.kid: Who looked after you as a baby?

options: Their older sisters, the worker bees
check.why: Worker bees are all female, and they feed the young bees in the hive. The queen lays the eggs.

setup.art: Sixteen cards face down on a floor in four rows of four.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the cards face down.

setup.art: Two cards turned face up: a drawing of a calf, and a drawing of a cow licking a calf.
setup.caption: 2. Find a baby and their carer.

projects.title: The Care Count: a three-day diary
projects.context: In this project you keep tally marks for three days. Each time someone cares for you, you make a mark. Each time you care for someone else, you make a mark in another colour. At the end, you find out how much caring goes on in your home, and in which direction.

materials.item: a sheet of paper with two columns: 'Someone cared for me' and 'I cared for someone'
two pencils or crayons of different colours

schedule.what: Make the chart. Make tally marks through the day: care you got, and care you gave.
Keep making marks. Write one example of each kind of care.
Count up the marks for all three days. Compare the two columns and talk about what you found.

projects.record: The tally chart for three days, with the totals.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with two columns, 'Someone cared for me' and 'I cared for someone', with tally marks in two colours.
setup.caption: 1. Make a two-column tally chart.

setup.art: A child watering a potted plant on a balcony, and making a tally mark on the chart stuck to the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Make a mark each time care happens.

flow.do: 1. Make the chart with your child. 2. Agree what counts: someone gave you food, helped you, comforted you, or you did that for someone, a pet or a plant. 3. Make marks through the day.
flow.say: Every time someone looks after you today, make a mark here. Every time you look after someone, make a mark there.
flow.kid: Make a mark when someone cares for you. Use the other colour when you care.

flow.do: Keep making marks. At the end of the day, your child writes one example in each column.
flow.say: What is one way someone cared for you today? What is one way you cared for someone?
flow.kid: Write one example in each column.

flow.do: Count up both columns. Compare them.
flow.say: Which column has more marks? Did you care for anyone? Who cares for the grown-ups?
flow.kid: Count both columns. Which has more? Why?

ask.q: Why does the 'cared for me' column have more marks?
good: Because I am still a child, and I need more care.
Because grown-ups cook and help me.

check.q: Kavya, a girl in Class 2, counted 30 marks for care she got and 12 for care she gave. What does that show?
options: Kavya gets more care than she gives, but she gives care too
check.why: Children need a lot of care, so they usually get more than they give. But 12 marks show that Kavya cares for others too.

challenges.title: Find Me in the Dark: design the easiest mouth to find
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the Find the Hungry Mouth test, yellow paper mouths were found more than dark ones in the dim nest. Now you design a paper mouth that is even easier to find in the dark.
challenges.problem: Can you make a paper chick mouth that a grown-up finds faster than a plain yellow one, in a dim nest?
constraints: The mouth must be the same size as the others: a bottle-cap circle.
Use only paper, crayons or sketch pens, glue, and silver foil if you have some.
The test is in the same dim room, on the same dark cloth.
materials: paper and crayons or sketch pens
a bottle cap to draw round
silver foil from a chocolate or a food packet, if you have some
the dark nest from the experiment
general: Use the brightest colour you have, like yellow or white.
Give the mouth a bright edge all the way round, like a sparrow chick's yellow corners.
Make the mouth a different colour from the cloth.
creative: Glue a ring of silver foil round the edge, so the mouth shines in any little light.
Make a white edge and a darker middle, so the edge stands out and the middle looks like a hole.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own mouth. Hide it in the nest with a plain yellow one. Ask a grown-up to find both in the dim light. Which did they find first? Try it three times.

flow.do: Read the challenge. Remind your child which mouths were easiest to find in the experiment.
flow.say: In the dark nest, yellow mouths were found most. Can you make a mouth that is even easier to find?
flow.kid: Make a mouth that is easy to find in the dark!

flow.do: Your child designs and makes one or two mouths.
flow.say: What would make a mouth stand out in the dark? Try an idea.
flow.kid: Make your mouth. What makes it stand out?
flow.parent: White and silver foil often work best. Let your child try their own idea first.

flow.do: Hide your child's mouth and a plain yellow mouth in the nest, in dim light. A grown-up looks in, and your child watches which one the grown-up touches first. Do it three times, mixing each time.
flow.say: I will look into the nest. Watch which mouth I touch first. We will try three times.
flow.kid: Watch the grown-up. Which mouth do they find first?

ask.q: Why was your mouth found first, or not?
good: The foil shone in the little light.
The white edge showed up on the dark cloth.

check.q: Which mouth is easiest to find on a dark cloth in dim light?
options: A white mouth with a bright edge
check.why: A light, bright mouth stands out against a dark cloth. Dark mouths look like the cloth, so they are hard to find.

setup.art: A child's hands gluing a ring of silver foil round a white paper circle the size of a bottle cap.
setup.caption: 1. Make your own mouth.

setup.art: A dark nest in a dim room with two paper circles, one plain yellow and one white with a silver edge, and a grown-up's hand reaching in.
setup.caption: 2. Test it against a plain yellow mouth.

items.p: Draw a line from each baby to their grown-up.
items.why: A calf grows into a cow, a kid into a goat, a chick into a hen, a puppy into a dog and a human baby into an adult human.
items.art: Five babies on the left and five adults on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Sort the babies: ready to walk soon after birth, or needs a lot of help?
items.why: Calves, ducklings and goat kids walk within a day. Sparrow chicks, kittens and human babies are born helpless and need care.
items.art: Six small drawings: a calf, a sparrow chick, a duckling, a kitten, a goat kid and a human baby.

items.p: Paper chick mouths of four colours, including yellow and black, are laid on a dark cloth in dim light. Draw them, and show which colour you think gets found most.
items.a: A dark nest with paper circles, and most chana on the yellow ones.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the dark cloth, the circles of four colours, and more chana on the bright yellow ones than on the black ones.
items.art: An empty box for drawing, with a dark rectangle at the bottom for the nest.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: in dim light, black paper mouths on a dark cloth are often missed. Why?
items.a: The black mouths look like the dark cloth, so they are hard to see in dim light.
items.why: A strong answer says the black mouths are the same colour as the cloth, and that the light is dim.

items.p: A newborn kitten's eyes are shut. When do they open?
opts: After about one to two weeks
items.why: A kitten's eyes open after about one to two weeks. Until then, the kitten finds the mother by smell and touch.

items.p: Only mother animals look after babies.
items.why: False. Sparrow fathers feed the chicks too. Langur aunts hold babies, and worker bees feed their young sisters. Many people care for a human baby.

items.p: A hen has 9 chicks. 4 chicks walk away to peck at seeds. How many chicks are still under her wings?
items.why: 9 take away 4 leaves 5 chicks under her wings.

items.p: Label the chick's picture: open mouth, yellow edge, shut eye, fluff.
a: open mouth: the big opening at the front
yellow edge: around the corners of the mouth
shut eye: on the side of the head
fluff: soft little feathers on the body
items.why: A young sparrow chick has a wide mouth with yellow edges, shut eyes and only a little fluff.
items.art: A drawing of a young sparrow chick begging, from the side, with four empty label lines.

items.p: Meena, aged 7, and her friend Joseph, aged 7, live in Mysuru. They are watching a hen with five chicks.

views.says: The chicks don't need their mother. They can walk and peck by themselves.
The chicks need their mother. She keeps them warm and safe.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one side and gives a reason, and says the other side is partly right. Chicks can walk and peck on the first day, so Meena is partly right. But the mother hen broods them to keep them warm and calls them away from danger, so Joseph is partly right too.
items.why: Both are true: chicks are born ready to walk and feed, but they still get care.

items.p: When a parent bird sits on small chicks to keep them warm, it is called ________.
items.why: Brooding means sitting over eggs or chicks to keep them warm. A hen broods her chicks under her wings.

items.p: A baby gecko waits in the nest for her mother to bring her insects.
items.why: False. A baby gecko hatches from the egg and hunts insects alone.

items.p: Sparrow chicks are fed in a dark hole. Crow chicks are fed in an open nest of sticks, in daylight. Which chicks need bright mouth edges more? Why?
items.a: The sparrow chicks, because their nest is dark and the parent must find their mouths without much light.
items.why: A strong answer uses the dark nest test: colour mattered in dim light, and hardly at all in bright light.

items.p: Paper chick mouths of different colours are laid on a dark cloth. Now the room is brightly lit. What do you think happens?
opts: Almost every mouth gets food, whatever the colour
items.why: In bright light, every colour is easy to see. So bright mouth colours matter most when the nest is dark.

items.p: Sort these into what a baby does to get care, and what a carer does.
items.why: Babies cry, beg and hold on. Carers feed, warm and clean. Both sides do something.

items.p: Draw yourself as a baby, doing one thing that helped someone look after you.
items.a: A baby crying, gripping a finger, smiling or reaching up.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a real baby signal: crying, gripping, smiling or reaching. These tell a carer what the baby needs.

items.p: Lakshmi, aged 8, and her grandmother live in Madurai. A tiny sparrow chick is sitting on the ground below a tree. The chick has feathers, but cannot fly far.

views.says: We must take the chick home and feed them, or they will die.
Leave the chick where they are. The parents are nearby and will keep feeding them.
Watch from far away for an hour. If no parent comes, or the chick is hurt, call a bird rescue group.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one view and gives a reason. Young birds who have just left the nest often sit on the ground while the parents still feed them, so the grandmother is often right. Lakshmi is right that the chick needs food, and Dr Farida is right that a hurt or alone chick needs help.
items.why: Fledglings out of the nest are usually still cared for by their parents. Watching first is the safest choice.

items.p: Three of these babies drink their mother's milk. Which one does not?
items.why: A chick is a bird. Birds do not make milk. Calves, kittens and human babies are mammals, and drink milk.

items.p: Label the stages of a human life, in order: baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult.
items.why: Humans go from baby to toddler to child to teenager to adult, and keep changing as they grow older.
items.art: Five people standing in a row from smallest to tallest, with five empty label lines.

items.p: A chick's open mouth, often with bright edges, is called the ________.
items.why: The gape is the open mouth of a chick. Many gapes have bright colours or edges.

items.p: In the dim nest, the yellow mouths got 2, 1 and 2 chana in three rounds. How many in all?
items.why: 2 and 1 make 3. 3 and 2 make 5.

items.p: A sparrow chick hatches with shut eyes and almost no feathers. Why can she not find her own food on the first day?
items.a: She cannot see, cannot fly and cannot walk far, so she needs her parents to bring food to the nest.
items.why: A strong answer uses what the chick looks like when she hatches: shut eyes and almost no feathers.

items.p: Priya, aged 9, and her brother Sameer, aged 7, live in Kolkata. They are talking about why chick mouths are bright.

views.says: Bright mouths help the parents find the chicks in the dark.
Bright mouths tell the parents which chick is hungriest.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what happens when coloured mouths are hidden in a dark nest. Then say what test could show if the other person is right.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence: in dim light, bright mouths are found more, so Priya's idea fits. For Sameer's idea, you would need to see if hungrier chicks have brighter mouths. Scientists have found both ideas can be true, in different birds.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. A good answer uses evidence for one side and suggests a fair test for the other.

items.p: Kavya lays coloured paper chick mouths on a white cloth instead of a dark one. Which mouths would be hardest to find now?
items.why: On a white cloth, yellow mouths are pale like the cloth, so they would be hardest to see. Black mouths would stand out. A mouth is easy to find when its colour is different from what is around it.

items.p: Design a nest for chicks in a dark hole. Draw the chicks with mouths that are easy for the parents to find.
items.a: A dark hole with chicks whose mouths have bright, light edges.
items.why: A strong drawing shows mouths that stand out against the dark: yellow, white or with a bright edge.

items.p: If a person touches a baby bird, the parents will always smell the person and leave the chick.
items.why: False. Most small birds have a weak sense of smell, and parents usually come back. But we still never touch nests, because it scares the parents and can hurt the chicks.

items.p: A sparrow chick begs harder when hungry. Why is that useful for the chick, and for the parents?
items.a: The hungry chick gets fed, and the parents know which chick needs food most, so they do not waste food.
items.why: A strong answer says something for both sides: the chick gets food, and the parent learns who needs it.

items.p: Sort these carers: does one carer look after the baby, or many?
items: a human baby in a big family
items.why: A mother cat and a mother tilapia do most of the care alone. Langur aunts, worker bees and human families share the care.

items.p: Label the ways a hen cares for her chicks: warming, leading to food, calling for danger, guarding.
a: leading to food: scratching the ground to show food
calling for danger: a sharp call when a hawk flies over
guarding: standing in front of the chicks
items.why: A hen broods her chicks, leads them to food, gives alarm calls and guards them.
items.art: Four small pictures of a hen with chicks, each with an empty label line.

items.p: Put the sparrow chick's life in order.
items: The chick leaves the nest and is still fed by the parents.
The egg is kept warm by the parents.
The chick hatches with shut eyes and no feathers.
The young sparrow finds food alone.
The chick grows feathers in the nest.
a: The egg is kept warm by the parents.
The chick hatches with shut eyes and no feathers.
The chick grows feathers in the nest.
The chick leaves the nest and is still fed by the parents.
The young sparrow finds food alone.
items.why: Egg, hatching, feathers, leaving the nest, then finding food alone. The parents care for the chick through all the early stages.

items.p: A scientist watches babies at home for many months. Which people do you think the babies will follow and hold on to most?
opts: Only the person who fed them
The people who came when they cried, talked and played with them
items.why: Babies held on most to the people who answered their signals. Feeding matters, but answering a baby's cries and smiles mattered most.

videos.title: A langur female takes a baby to practise being a mother

videos.check: Found by search: "A Langur Female Steals a Baby to Practice Being a Mom" by Smithsonian Channel, 3 minutes, 26 seconds. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: Which of these is a sign that a young animal is growing up?
quiz.why: Growing up means getting bigger and changing. A kitten gets bigger, opens her eyes and learns to hunt.

quiz.p: When does a calf usually stand up?
opts: Within about an hour of birth
quiz.why: A calf stands within about an hour, so she can follow her mother.

quiz.p: How does a sparrow chick look when they first hatch?
quiz.why: Sparrow chicks hatch almost bare and with shut eyes. They need their parents to feed them.

quiz.p: Which is a way a hen cares for her chicks?
opts: She broods them under her wings to keep them warm
She leaves them alone on the first day
quiz.why: A hen broods her chicks under her wings. Birds do not make milk.

quiz.p: Who helps a langur mother look after her baby?
opts: Other female langurs, who take turns holding the baby
quiz.why: Among langurs, other females take turns holding and carrying a new baby.

quiz.p: What does a hungry sparrow chick do when a parent lands at the nest?
opts: Stretches up, cheeps and opens a wide mouth
quiz.why: The chick begs. Begging tells the parent the chick is hungry and where to put the food.

quiz.p: How does a human baby help their own care?
quiz.why: Babies cry when they need something, grip fingers and smile at faces. Carers answer these signals.

quiz.p: In a game, paper chick mouths of different colours are laid in a dark box. A 'parent' drops chana into the ones it finds. Why should the mouths be mixed up before every round?
opts: So no colour is always in the best place
So the chana do not roll
quiz.why: Mixing makes the test fair. If yellow was always in the middle, it might be found because of the place, not the colour.

quiz.p: In the dim nest, yellow mouths got 5 chana in all and black mouths got 1. What does that show?
opts: Yellow mouths are easier to find in dim light
quiz.why: The yellow mouths were found five times as often. In dim light, bright colours stand out against a dark nest.

quiz.p: Which of these is true about humans?
opts: Humans are animals whose young need care for many years
Human babies walk on the first day
quiz.why: Humans are animals, and mammals. Human babies need care for many years, longer than most animals.

quiz.p: About how long does a human take to grow up?
quiz.why: A human takes about 18 years to grow up. A mouse takes about two months and a cow about two years.

applications: People who rescue baby birds feed them with soft tweezers or a small brush, aiming into the open gape just as the parent would.
In some zoos, keepers feed chicks using a puppet shaped like the parent's head, so the chicks grow up knowing their own kind.
Nurses who care for newborn babies watch for the baby's signals, such as turning the head and sucking a fist, to tell when the baby is hungry.
Nature Forever Society, started by Mohammed Dilawar in Nashik, gives out nest boxes so that house sparrows have dark holes to raise their chicks in city buildings.

spotted.text: House sparrows carrying grass into a gap behind a meter box or an AC pipe in a building in Kochi or Pune.
spotted.art: A sparrow flying into a gap beside an AC pipe on a building wall, with grass in her beak.

open_questions.q: Why do human children take so long to grow up?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have several ideas: big brains that take years to grow, a lot to learn, and many carers who share the work. They still argue about which matters most.

open_questions.q: What does a parent animal feel when the young beg?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can see how parents act, and can measure some chemicals in the body. What the feeling is like for a sparrow or a cow is still unknown.

open_questions.q: Why do chick mouths have the colours they do?
open_questions.why_open: In some birds, bright mouths seem to help parents find chicks in the dark. In others, the colour seems to tell the parent how hungry or healthy the chick is. Scientists are still testing both ideas.

maths.problem: In the dim nest, the yellow mouths got 5 chana in all and the black mouths got 1. How many more did the yellow mouths get?
maths.explain: Start at 1 and count up to 5: that is 4 more. So the yellow mouths were found much more often than the black ones.
maths.context: This is about the Find the Hungry Mouth test, where you fed paper mouths in a dim nest.
maths.why_maths: Finding the difference shows how big the effect of the colour was, not just which colour won.

maths.problem: Kavya, the girl in the sparrow story, watched the nest for 10 minutes. Each parent brought food 4 times. How many feeds did the chicks get?
maths.explain: There are 2 parents, and each brought food 4 times. That is two groups of 4. 4 and 4 make 8.
maths.context: This is about Kavya's story, where she counted how often the sparrow parents came to the nest.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal groups shows how much work two parents do together.

maths.problem: A calf walks after about 1 hour. A kitten walks after about 3 weeks. A human baby walks after about 12 months. Put them in order from first to last.
maths.explain: An hour is much shorter than a week, and a week is much shorter than a month. So 1 hour comes first, then 3 weeks, then 12 months.
maths.context: This is about the Walking Line activity, where you guessed when each baby first walks.
maths.why_maths: To compare these times, we must think about the units (hours, weeks and months), not only the numbers.

maths.problem: In the Care Count project, Rahul, a boy of six, made these marks in one day. Care he got: |||| |||| (two groups of 4). Care he gave: |||. Which column has more marks, and how many more?
maths.answer: 'Care he got' has 8 marks and 'care he gave' has 3. Care he got has 5 more.
maths.explain: Count each group of tally marks: 4 and 4 make 8, and the other column has 3. 8 take away 3 is 5. Children get more care than they give, but they give some too.
maths.context: This is about the Care Count project, where you made tally marks each time care happened.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks let us count things that happen through a whole day, and then compare.

science: Cambridge Primary Science Learner's Book 2 (2nd edition), Unit 4.2 'Growing': young animals, including humans, change as they grow into adults; stages of human life.

Nestling mouth colour and detectability: P. Heeb, T. Schwander and S. Faoro, 'Nestling detectability affects parental feeding preferences in a cavity-nesting bird', Animal Behaviour 66 (2003) 637-642 (great tits; in dim nests, red-painted mouths were less detected than yellow; no effect in bright nests).
Mouth colour as a signal of need or condition: N. Saino and colleagues on barn swallow nestlings (around 2000-2003).
Parent-offspring conflict: R. L. Trivers, 'Parent-offspring conflict', American Zoologist 14 (1974).
House sparrow breeding: both parents feed nestlings; young leave the nest at about 14-16 days and are fed by the parents for some days after. Nestlings have yellow gape flanges.
Hanuman langur infant handling by females other than the mother: Phyllis Jay (Dolhinow) in north India (1960s); Sarah Blaffer Hrdy at Mount Abu, Rajasthan (1970s).
King cobra females build leaf-litter nests and guard the eggs. Mozambique tilapia females brood eggs and young in the mouth.

Attachment: M. D. S. Ainsworth, Infancy in Uganda (1967), fieldwork 1954-55 near Kampala. H. R. Schaffer and P. E. Emerson, 'The development of social attachments in infancy', Monographs of the Society for Research in Child Development (1964), 60 Glasgow infants.
Human social smiling appears at about 6 weeks; independent walking typically between about 9 and 18 months (WHO Motor Development Study, 2006).
Kittens' eyes open at about 7-14 days; puppies' at about 10-14 days. Calves and goat kids usually stand within an hour of birth.
Mencius 2A:6 (the child about to fall into a well). Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8.

roots.context: We have learnt how young animals grow up, how they are cared for, and how they beg to be fed. Now we ask what the dark nest test tells us about care, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In your dim nest, yellow mouths got the most chana, and dark mouths were often missed. In bright light, every colour was found. Sparrow chicks in dark holes have bright yellow mouth edges. So a chick helps to get fed, by being easy for a parent to find.
deep_truth.habit: We picture a baby as helpless, with care flowing one way, from the parent to the baby. But babies beg, call, cry, grip and show bright mouths, and the carer answers. Care is something the baby and the carer do together.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Find the Hungry Mouth test, yellow paper mouths were fed far more often than black ones in dim light, but not in bright light. Scientists found the same with real great tit chicks in 2003: in dim nests, parents fed yellow-painted mouths more than red-painted ones.

three.who_am_i: You were once a baby who cried, gripped and smiled. People answered you, and you grew. You helped make your own care.
three.what_is_life: A young life grows because others feed and protect them, and because the young one asks for what they need.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of babies asking and carers answering: sparrows in walls, langurs on temples, people in every home.

roots.thread: Every animal alive today, including you, was once young. Many were fed by someone else. A sparrow chick's yellow mouth and a parent's search for it work as one: neither alone gets the food where it must go. A human baby's cry and a grandmother's arms work the same way. The many babies of the world each grow up inside a web of others who answer them.

teachings.teaching: Mencius, a Chinese thinker, said that anyone who suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well feels alarm and wants to help. Nobody has to teach them this feeling.
teachings.link: A carer answers a baby's signals quickly, often before thinking. In this unit, a parent sparrow flies to the open yellow mouth, and a grandmother turns to a crying baby.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught: just as a mother protects her only child with her own life, so we should grow a boundless kindness towards all living beings.
teachings.link: In this unit, care is often shared beyond one parent: langur aunts, worker bee sisters and the many people around a human baby. The teaching asks us to stretch that care to every being.

science.text: In a 2003 study with great tits, scientists painted the chicks' mouths yellow or red. In dim nests, parents fed yellow-painted chicks more. In bright nests, the colour made no difference.
Why chick mouths are coloured is still argued about. In some birds the colour helps parents find the chicks, and in others the colour seems to show how hungry or healthy the chick is.

other_view.who: Many biologists who study animal behaviour
other_view.view: A parent bird feeding an open mouth is a fixed, automatic response to a signal, like a key opening a lock. In this view, neither chick nor parent needs to feel or decide anything for the feeding to happen.

practice.title: Bubble Nest Breath
practice.say: Sit down and put both hands on your belly. Breathe in slowly, and feel your belly push your hands out. Breathe out slowly, as if blowing a soap bubble. Do it three times. Now think of someone who cared for you when you were small. Breathe in and out once more, and think of someone you care for now.

how_we_found_out.story: About 70 years ago, many doctors and scientists thought babies love whoever feeds them. They said a baby holds on to the mother because she gives milk. Some even told parents not to pick up a crying baby too often. In the 1950s, a scientist called Mary Ainsworth went to villages in Uganda, near Kampala. She sat in homes and watched mothers and babies for many months. She saw babies crawl after their mothers, cry when they left and smile when they came back. Babies held on most to people who came quickly when they cried. In Glasgow, in Scotland, Rudolph Schaffer and Peggy Emerson visited 60 babies again and again through their first year. Many babies held on most to someone who played with them and answered them, even when another person did more of the feeding. So babies do not only want food. They want people who answer their signals.
how_we_found_out.who: Mary Ainsworth, a scientist from Canada and the United States, working in Uganda (1954 to 1955); Rudolph Schaffer and Peggy Emerson in Glasgow, Scotland (1964)
how_we_found_out.when: Ainsworth watched babies in Uganda in 1954 and 1955 and wrote her book in 1967. Schaffer and Emerson published their study in 1964.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That babies love whoever feeds them, and that picking up a crying baby too often spoils them. Watching real babies showed that babies hold on most to the people who answer their cries and play with them.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman scientist with a notebook sitting on a mat in a village home, watching a mother and a crawling baby who reaches towards the mother.

playtest: Played both games in my head with 2 and with 4 players: the sorting race has every player racing and says what happens when nobody is right, and the memory game's 16 cards are all listed. Followed the dark-nest experiment in a flat: each mouth gets only one chana, so the example numbers in the parent notes, maths, quiz and worksheets were impossible and now fit (for example 5 for yellow and 1 for black). Fixed the walking line (a missing 'one hour' mark and the card list), replaced three copies of the same ordering and 'why humans take long' questions, introduced Kavya and Rahul where they appear, cut the jokes to 8 real ones, and removed an unneeded safety warning and an internal source note. On a second walk-through I made the kitten and puppy walking age one plain figure (about three weeks) in all places, added picking the chana back up between rounds, swapped two weak jokes, and made the Ainsworth question clearer. The three video ids are still to be found.
